title: Europe’s Ancient Landscapes May Have Been More Open Than We Thought
paragraphs: A team from Aarhus University in Denmark studied how the landscapes of Europe looked in the past. They used many kinds of evidence, for example old pollen, charcoal from fires, and the bones and teeth of animals.

The team found that Europe was not covered by thick, dark forest for most of the last 20 million years. Instead, it was a mix of trees, open places and flowers. Big plant-eating animals, such as elephants, rhinos, wild cattle and bison, helped to keep these places open.

The scientists think this is important for nature today. They believe that planting only dense forests may not be the best idea. They say people should also protect open places and bring back large animals. The study was published in the journal Biological Conservation.

questions.q: What kinds of evidence did the team use?
questions.a: Pollen, charcoal, and animal bones and teeth.

questions.q: What do the scientists want to protect?
questions.a: Open places and large animals, not only dense forests.
